title: Detect Abuse of Container APIs for Credential Access
shortTitle: Detect Abuse of Container APIs for Credential Access
summary: This strategy detects access to container management interfaces that exposes credentials, covering T1552.007 Container API under Unsecured Credentials. The technique matters because whoever can reach the container daemon socket or the cluster application programming interface can read environment variables, mounted secret files, and service account tokens that were never meant to leave the container boundary. Useful telemetry comes from audit logging on the container runtime and on the cluster control plane, plus host process records that show who connected to the socket. The common failure is that these interfaces are frequently unauthenticated on the host, so the request looks like ordinary local administration and only the calling process and its lineage separate abuse from routine operations.

beginner.definition: This detection watches who talks to the container management interface. That interface can list containers and read the secrets inside them. An attacker who reaches it can steal passwords without touching the application itself. The rule looks at the process that connects and at the secrets it reads.
beginner.whyItMatters: Containers often keep passwords in environment variables or in mounted files. The container tool can print those values on request. If a normal user account can reach that tool, the passwords are only one command away. Many teams protect the network but forget the local socket. This detection helps close that gap.
howItWorks: The container runtime writes an audit record for every request made to its management socket.
The cluster control plane writes a similar record for every call to its application programming interface, or API.
The detection reads those records and looks for requests that list or inspect secret objects.
It then finds the host process that made the request, using the process identifier in the record.
A request that comes from the platform controller is normal, because the platform does this every day.
A request that comes from a shell or a script inside another container is treated as suspicious.
beginner.example: Picture a hospital ward with a locked medicine cupboard. The key hangs on a hook beside it, because nurses need the cupboard many times a day. A visitor who takes the key and opens the cupboard looks exactly like a nurse from across the room. What tells the two apart is the uniform and the time on the sign in sheet. In the same way, a request to the container interface looks harmless on its own. The process that made the request and the account it used give you the uniform and the sign in sheet.
takeaways: The container management socket is a credential store, and it is often unauthenticated.
Alert on the process and account behind the request, not on the request alone.
Audit logging must be enabled first, or this detection sees nothing at all.

objectives: Describe how container interfaces expose environment variables and mounted secrets.
Identify the audit events that a container runtime and a cluster control plane produce.
Correlate an API request with the host process and account behind it.
Distinguish platform components from user shells that call the same interface.
Recommend audit logging and socket permission baselines as preventive controls.
dataSources: Kubernetes API server audit logs recording get and list requests for Secret objects
Container runtime daemon audit records for requests sent to the management socket
Linux auditd records for connect and open calls against the container runtime socket path
Sysmon for Linux process creation events with parent image and command line
Host endpoint sensor records of processes that mount or read container socket files
logic: The pattern is a request to a container management interface that returns secret content, made by a process that is not part of the platform itself. The fields that must be correlated are the API verb and object type, the requesting identity and source address, the target namespace or container, and the host process identifier that opened the socket connection. The malicious case differs from the benign one mainly by identity and origin: reconciliation controllers, backup jobs, and monitoring agents read secret metadata from the platform identity inside the cluster, while an interactive shell on a host, a process inside a different container, or a workload service account reading environment variables of another workload is not routine. Reading the content of a secret rather than its metadata is the sharpest discriminator, because very few legitimate processes need the value itself.
pseudoQuery:
# title: Container API Secret Read by Unusual Process
# logsource:
#   product: linux
# detection:
#   selection:
#     event_type: api_request
#     object: secret
#     verb:
#       - get
#       - list
#   filter_platform:
#     user|startswith: 'system:serviceaccount:platform:'
#   condition: selection and not filter_platform
# level: high
falsePositives: Cluster backup operators that list secrets as part of a scheduled vault export
Continuous integration runners that read a deployment secret at build time
Monitoring agents that inspect secret metadata for expiry and rotation checks
Administrators troubleshooting from a jump host with an interactive command line session
Secret management controllers that sync values into an external vault
tuningNotes: Restrict the rule to the verbs that return secret content, because list and watch calls generate most of the noise, and exclude the platform service accounts that reconciliation controllers use. Baseline which users and service accounts read secrets over two weeks, allow that set by name, and keep everything else at high severity. Narrowing this way loses visibility into a compromised but legitimate reader, so pair the rule with an anomaly check on the volume of secret reads per account and per namespace.
